newsitem.title: USA: U.S. appoints Holbrooke special emissary on Cyprus.
newsitem.headline: U.S. appoints Holbrooke special emissary on Cyprus.

text.p: President Bill Clinton appointed Richard Holbrooke, who mediated the Bosnian peace deal, as his special emissary for Cyprus on Wednesday in a sign of U.S. commitment to a settlement on the divided island.
"President Clinton has named Ambassador Richard Holbrooke as the new U.S. special presidential emissary on Cyprus," State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns told reporters.

Burns said the appointment represented "a rebirth and a renewal" of the U.S. mediation effort between the Greek and Turkish communities, divided since 1974 when Turkish troops invaded the island in response to a pro-Greek coup.
"This appointment of one of our most capable negotiators demonstrates our commitment to help promote a final political settlement on Cyprus," Burns said.
Holbrooke will replace Richard Beattie, named by Secretary of State Madeleine Albright last month as her adviser on incorporating three foreign affairs agencies into the State Department.
Burns said the United States had no illusions about the toughness and complexity of the challenge. "That is why we are bringing in our toughest negotiator," he said.
"(Holbrooke) does not expect any imminent breakthroughs in this assignment. He's also going to take it slow at the beginning. He's not planning any trips to the region in the next week or two."

Burns noted that President Glafkos Clerides of Cyprus and Turkish Cypriot leader Rauf Denktash were due to meet in July in New York and said Washington strongly urged all parties to work for a comprehensive, permanent settlement on the island.

Holbrooke, outspoken, blunt and dogged, made his name by pressuring warring Balkan forces to reach peace agreements to end the 43-month Bosnia war at Dayton, Ohio, in 1995. In February of last year he resigned as assistant secretary of state and took a job with Credit Suisse First Boston bank in New York, which he still holds.
Burns said he would not take the Cyprus post on a full-time basis. He would work on it about one week a month, retaining his main job with the bank, and appoint a negotiating team to work full-time.

The New York talks between Clerides and Denktash, whose Turkish Cypriot breakaway state in northern Cyprus is recognised only by Ankara, will be their first face-to-face encounter for nearly three years. Some 30,000 Turkish troops are stationed in northern Cyprus.
